Orgalyst: a conversational analysis system for organoid bright-field images

A domain toolkit that reproduces every number without any large language model, and an assistant that puts it in the hands of bench scientists.

CategoryEnd-to-End SystemTeamXiaoyan Li (AI / computer vision / LLM applications, project lead); Liwen Xu and Xuzheng Fu (biology: organoid culture and morphological interpretation, responsible for requirements and review of results); Cuicui JiangCodehttps://github.com/xiaoyanLi629/orgalyst (MIT)Weightshttps://huggingface.co/XiaoyanLi/orgalyst-weightsDataOrgLine (Zenodo 16355179, CC-BY-4.0); no private data was used

1 Abstract

Organoid and organ-on-a-chip experiments produce large numbers of bright-field micrographs every day, and the three questions asked most often are how many, how big, and has anything changed. Existing tools are either scripts that need tuning or software that segments but leaves statistics and record-keeping to the user, so turning a folder of images into a report that can go into a lab notebook still costs half a day. Orgalyst splits this chain into two layers. The lower layer is a deterministic toolkit, orgalyst: Cellpose segmentation with organ-specific weights, YOLO counting with calibrated confidence thresholds, morphometry, quality control, group statistics, growth curves, single-file HTML reports and a run manifest that records input hashes, weight hashes, parameters and software versions. The upper layer is a conversational assistant built on the Claude Agent SDK that calls these tools through MCP, so a bench scientist can go from images to report in one sentence while every number is still computed by the toolkit. We ran five groups of experiments on the public OrgLine dataset (eight sources, five organs). After per-organ fine-tuning, segmentation AP50 reaches 0.967, 0.812 and 0.815 on brain, intestine and colon (zero-shot cyto3: 0.005, 0.544, 0.405). A three-organ YOLO11m detector reaches mAP50 0.936 to 0.995, and calibrating the counting threshold on the validation set lowers the counting error on lung organoids from 0.235 to 0.168. On 240 brain organoid images the automatic area agrees with expert annotation at Spearman 0.963 with a median relative error of 1.9%. In an end-to-end benchmark of 12 natural-language tasks the assistant passed 12 of 12 at an average of 113 s per task. We also report honestly where cross-organ generalisation ends, where the system falls short on pancreatic cancer organoids, and why a Cellpose-SAM comparison brought no gain.

2 Problem definition and application scenario

Organoids are miniature tissues grown from stem cells in a three-dimensional environment; organ-on-a-chip devices place such tissues into microfluidic hardware that mimics physiological conditions. In both cases the cheapest, least invasive and most frequent way to observe them is the bright-field microscope: take a picture every day or every few hours and see how they are growing. The analysis these pictures need is very fixed. Count how many organoids are in an image, measure the size and shape of each, compare treatment groups, connect measurements of the same organoid over time into a growth curve, and finally write it all up as a report that can go into the lab record and be checked by someone else.

The bottleneck is not the algorithm. Tools such as Cellpose, OrganoID and OrgaSegment already segment organoids well, and the OrgLine dataset has even unified eight public sources into one format. What actually stops bench scientists are three things. First, the tools are for people who write code: an environment has to be installed, a model chosen, a diameter parameter tuned, and when organoids in one image differ tenfold in size the default parameters fail while the scientist does not know which knob to turn. Second, segmentation is only the first step; the measuring, statistics, plotting and report writing that follow are reinvented in every lab, inconsistently, so results cannot be compared. Third, nothing is recorded: three months later a reviewer asks which model version and which parameters produced this area, and most people cannot answer.

Orgalyst targets biologists who run organoid or organ-on-a-chip experiments and do not write code. Success is defined by three criteria: a scientist gets a complete analysis report using natural language alone; every number in that report can be recomputed from the command line in an environment without any language model, and agrees with the expert annotation shipped with a public dataset; and the system says when it is unsure rather than returning a wrong number that looks precise. The third criterion is why quality control and the run manifest are first-class parts of the toolkit rather than add-ons.

3 Data

All experiments use OrgLine (Zenodo 16355179, CC-BY-4.0), which unifies eight published organoid image datasets into an instance segmentation subset (InstanceSeg) and a detection subset (OrgDet). Segmentation covers four organs: brain (Schröter et al. 2024), intestine (OrgaSegment), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, pdac (OrganoID and OrganoIDNet) and colon (OrgaExtractor). Detection covers intestine (Tellu, OrgaQuant, OrgaSegment), brain and lung (Deep-LUMEN). We used no private data from any company or laboratory and added no annotations.

scripts/prepare_data.py converts the raw data into 8-bit PNG images and uint16 instance masks (one integer label per organoid) plus YOLO text labels for detection; true-colour bright-field images keep RGB, images whose three channels are identical become grey, and 16-bit images are stretched to 8 bits between the 1st and 99th percentiles. The segmentation subset keeps OrgLine's own split; the detection subset is split 70 / 15 / 15 at random (seed 0) and the split files ship with the repository. A physical pixel size is documented only for the brain dataset (3.1646 µm/px for Lab A images 1024 px wide, 2.9940 µm/px for Lab B images 1388 px wide). The other source papers give the instrument and objective but no calibration; we do not guess, so morphometry for those sources is reported in pixels and the report says so.

Each brain image contains exactly one organoid (the 240 test images come from 4 clones × 3 individuals × 10 time points × 2 laboratories), which makes it natural material for growth curves and for the comparison with expert-annotated area. The pdac test images contain more than 500 small instances each while training images average 68; this in-domain shift is the main source of failure discussed in sections 7 and 8. Colon has only 15 training images and no masks in its validation set.

4 Methods and system

4.1 Architecture

The system has two layers. The toolkit layer, orgalyst, is an ordinary Python package with the command-line entry point python -m orgalyst analyze | count | track | report and needs no language model. Every run leaves a directory containing manifest.json (md5 of each input file, model identifier and weight hash, all parameters, numpy / torch / cellpose / ultralytics versions, GPU model, step-by-step log), tables/ (per-instance features, summary, QC, comparison and growth tables), masks/, overlays/ and a single-file report.html. The assistant layer is a slimmed copy of BioAgent, the Claude Agent SDK assistant we built earlier for our laboratory (permission gatekeeper, terminal and web interfaces). The toolkit is exposed to it through one MCP server (orgalyst/mcp_server.py, stdio transport) with six tools: list_models, analyze_images, count_organoids, compare_groups, growth_curves, run_summary (plus list_runs). The assistant's system prompt states which tool to use when, that answers must distinguish pixels from micrometres, and that border-touching instances are excluded by default. The assistant does not look at pixels or compute numbers; it only interprets the request, chooses parameters and explains the results.

4.2 Segmentation: the Cellpose architecture and organ-specific weights

Segmentation uses Cellpose (Stringer et al., Nature Methods 2021). Its core is not a particular network but a reformulation of instance segmentation as regression of a flow field. At training time, heat is diffused from the centre of every annotated instance, giving each pixel the direction towards the centre of the instance it belongs to. A U-Net with residual blocks and skip connections learns to predict these two direction maps and one map of whether a pixel is an object at all. At inference every foreground pixel is moved along the direction map for about 200 steps, and pixels that converge to the same point form one instance. This design handles touching, non-convex and very differently sized objects naturally, and it makes the backbone replaceable: Cellpose-SAM is the same group's 2025 version with a ViT backbone.

Cellpose has an easily overlooked precondition: the network is trained at a scale where objects are about 30 pixels wide, so before inference the typical diameter of objects in the image must be estimated and the image rescaled accordingly. Getting the diameter wrong has direct consequences. Too small, and the image is enlarged so one organoid is split into several; too large, and the image shrinks so all organoids blur into one. Cellpose ships a size model that regresses the diameter from the network's style vector, but it was trained on cell images and predicts about 30 pixels for brain organoids 400 pixels wide, which is why zero-shot brain AP50 is only 0.005.

Figure 2c · Same intestinal organoid image, same model, only the diameter estimate changed.

Our approach is to load organ-specific weights and pick a diameter strategy per organ. The weights come from continuing to train the generalist cyto3 on each OrgLine organ for 200 epochs (section 6); during training Cellpose stores the median instance diameter of the training set in the weights (diam_labels). Four diameter strategies are registered per organ in orgalyst/config.py: model uses the training diameter stored in the weights (colon); sizemodel estimates the diameter per image with the cyto3 size model (intestine and pdac, whose images differ in magnification); refine runs inference twice, first at the training diameter and then at the median equivalent diameter of the objects found in the first pass, clamped to 0.25 to 4 times (brain, whose organoids grow almost fivefold in area between day 2 and day 30, so no single diameter works at both ends); per_image_gt uses the ground-truth diameter and serves only as an experimental upper bound. Unknown organs fall back to zero-shot cyto3 with the size model, and the report marks the result as "generalist model, lower accuracy".

Figure 3 · On brain organoids the generalist model fails because of scale, not appearance; the organ-specific weights remember the scale.

4.3 Counting by detection

When the user only asks how many, segmentation is wasteful: a 2048-pixel intestinal image takes seconds to segment and well under a second to detect. We trained YOLO11m on the OrgLine detection subset (input 1024, 100 epochs) and compared three single-organ models with one three-organ joint model; the joint model matched or beat every single-organ model, so the system keeps only that one. A parameter that is easy to overlook in counting is the confidence threshold: the ultralytics default of 0.25 is designed for computing mAP and deliberately keeps many low-confidence boxes, which over-counts by about twenty percent when used directly. We swept the threshold from 0.05 to 0.90 on each organ's validation set and kept the value with the lowest mean relative counting error (intestine 0.50, brain 0.45, lung 0.40; 0.45 for unknown organs, the pooled optimum), wrote it into the configuration, and used the test set only to report the final error.

4.4 Morphometry, quality control, statistics and growth curves

Measurement uses scikit-image regionprops: area, equivalent diameter, perimeter, circularity (4π·area / perimeter²), solidity (area / convex-hull area), aspect ratio and whether the instance touches the image border; when a pixel size is given the micrometre columns are added. Border-touching instances are incomplete, so summary statistics exclude them by default and the report states how many. Quality control works at two levels. Image level: sharpness (variance of the Laplacian), uneven illumination (coefficient of variation of local means) and the fraction of saturated pixels. Instance level: test-time augmentation with flips and rotations, comparing the segmentation of the original image with those of 4 dihedral transforms; an instance recovered in fewer than half of the transforms is flagged "low confidence" and drawn in orange in the report. The user thus receives not just a number but also which instances are doubtful. Statistics compare groups: Mann-Whitney U for two groups, Kruskal-Wallis for more, Cliff's delta as effect size, Holm correction across metrics, with box plots and a comparison table. Growth curves connect the per-image median area over individuals, time points and groups from metadata, giving each individual's fold change relative to its first time point and the mean curve per group.

4.5 Agent orchestration and record-keeping

On receiving a request the assistant first breaks the work into three to eight steps with its task-list tool and tells the user the plan, then calls the tools step by step. The judgements it actually has to make are few: which organ the images are (if unstated, use generic and say so), whether a pixel size is known (if not, report pixels and never invent one), whether the user wants counting or measurement, whether QC is wanted, and where group and time-point information lives. Every tool call writes into the output directory of the current conversation, and answers cite the run directory and the report path. The permission gatekeeper (agent/bioagent/permissions.py) keeps raw-data directories read-only and forbids access to other accounts' directories and to secrets; the user chooses a confirmation mode per conversation (confirm everything, confirm only dangerous commands, fully automatic, or read-only). The assistant also keeps a per-account long-term memory (which project the user is working on, usual data paths, pixel calibrations and preferences, summarised automatically at the end of a session), and the web edition supports multiple accounts with per-account spending limits and an administrator panel; memory was disabled during the E5 benchmark so that tasks stayed independent.

Open-model path. The Claude Agent SDK can be pointed through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at any gateway that speaks the Anthropic Messages API; agent/README.md documents a LiteLLM-in-front-of-vLLM configuration, and the E5 benchmark script can be run once per backend. For lack of time this report gives results for the Claude backend only, which section 8 lists as a limitation.

4.6 Usage flow and outputs

A typical session goes like this. The scientist types, in the web or terminal interface, "analyse the 4 intestinal organoid images under /data/exp3, do a morphological analysis and generate a report". The assistant lists its plan (confirm organ and pixel size, call the analysis tool, read the summary, write the answer), then calls analyze_images(images="/data/exp3", organ="intestine", name="exp3"). The toolkit segments, measures and builds the report within tens of seconds and returns the run directory and summary; the assistant turns the total, per-image counts, and the medians and interquartile ranges of area and circularity into a table and gives the report path. The end of the assistant's answer to this task in the E5 benchmark reads as follows (excerpt, translated). It states the units, points out that it did not invent a pixel size, suggests checking the overlays first, and says plainly that "201 is a model output with no accuracy guarantee", which is exactly the judgement we want the assistant to show:

"Note: all sizes are in pixels, not micrometres. You did not provide pixel_size_um and I have not invented a calibration. … I suggest looking through the 4 overlay images in overlays/ first. This run used the intestine-specific model, but without manual annotation as a gold standard, 201 is still just a model output with no accuracy guarantee."

5 As an analysis assistant: what can be asked, and how it works

Seen together, the toolkit and the assistant present the user with one assistant that knows how to analyse organoid images: the scientist describes the task in plain language, the assistant follows a standard procedure to call the tools, checks the results, reports in a fixed format, and leaves the report and data in the output directory of the conversation. It is not a chatbot with a few functions attached; it is an analysis protocol built into an assistant. Below we describe what can be asked, what procedure is followed, and what the interface looks like.

5.2 What procedure is followed

Tools alone are not enough. When the assistant should ask what, what to run first, how to check and how to report is written down as a reusable procedure, agent/skillpack/skills/organoid-analysis/SKILL.md, loaded automatically as a local skill of the Claude Agent SDK. It activates whenever the user mentions organoid image analysis and can also be invoked explicitly with /organoid-analysis. It prescribes four steps. First, confirm three prerequisites (organ type, pixel size, and whether the user wants counts, morphology or a comparison; ask for whatever is missing, but do not block a simple task). Second, choose tools from those prerequisites (counting goes to detection, everything else to segmentation; enable QC for small batches or when the user cares about reliability; attach statistics when group or time-point information exists). Third, check the returned values before answering (a per-image count of 0 or an outlier triggers a look at the overlay; the number of border-excluded and low-confidence instances must appear in the answer). Fourth, report in a fixed six-part format (one-sentence conclusion; per-image table with medians and interquartile ranges; units and exclusions; statistical conclusion; output paths; at most two next-step suggestions). The skill also lists prohibitions: no micrometre figures without a pixel size, no recomputing in Python what a tool already reported, no re-running the same batch. The assistant's behaviour therefore no longer depends on how well each prompt is written, and the same procedure carries over to a different model backend.

The effect shows in two ways. Answers have a fixed skeleton: prerequisites first (organ, units), then the conclusion and table, then paths and suggestions, as in the answer quoted in section 7.5. And the assistant says no when it should: no micrometre numbers without a pixel size, generalist-model results labelled as lower accuracy, outlying per-image counts checked against the overlay instead of copied. These behaviours live in the skill and the system prompt, not in the user's ability to ask well.

5.3 Interface

6 Implementation details

Hardware: one AutoDL cloud instance with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 D (32 GB) and a container memory limit of 62 GB. Software: Python 3.10, torch 2.14.0+cu130, cellpose 3.1.1.3, ultralytics 8.4.152, numpy 2.0.2, scikit-image 0.25. Segmentation fine-tuning: initialised from cyto3, 200 epochs per organ, learning rate 0.1 (Cellpose's default SGD), batch size 8; wall time 74 min for brain, 31 for pdac, 22 for intestine, 1.4 for colon. The cross-organ experiments cap each organ at 500 training images (the full four-organ set of 2395 images exceeds the container memory and is killed silently, one of the pitfalls we hit). Detection: initialised from yolo11m.pt, input 1024, batch 8, 100 epochs; 32 to 65 min per single-organ model and 126 min for the joint model. The Cellpose-SAM comparison ran in a separate cellpose 4 environment with batch 2, learning rate 1e-5, 100 epochs: 96 min for pdac and 25 for intestine. Measured per-stage timings are in Table 6-1.

Table 6-1 · Per-stage timing (scripts/bench_timing.py, results/timing.json; RTX 5090 D, intestine weights + sizemodel). On CPU only, segmenting the 512px image takes 14 s, still usable for small batches. Report generation (histograms and thumbnails) adds about 2 to 5 s.

The MCP interface is implemented with FastMCP; tool signatures are as follows (all parameters have defaults, all return JSON): analyze_images(images, organ="generic", pixel_size_um=None, name, diam_mode=None, limit=0, make_report=True, qc=False, meta_csv=None); count_organoids(images, organ="generic", name, conf=None, limit=0); compare_groups(run_dir, groups, metrics=None, exclude_border=True); growth_curves(run_dir, meta_csv=None, pattern=None, metric=None); run_summary(run_dir); list_models(); list_runs(limit=20). At start-up the MCP server redirects stdout to stderr and keeps a private handle for the protocol stream, so that print statements inside the underlying libraries cannot corrupt the protocol, a practice we adopted when integrating the Biomni tool library.

7 Experiments and results

7.1 E1 segmentation: zero-shot, per-organ fine-tuning, diameter strategy and cross-organ generalisation

The metric is instance-level AP50 (a predicted instance matches a ground-truth instance at IoU ≥ 0.5, computed with cellpose.metrics.average_precision); AP75 and AP90 are also reported to reflect boundary quality. Table 1 gives the main results.

Organ (test images)cyto3 zero-shotPer-organ fine-tuned (model diameter)Fine-tuned + per-image strategy (system default)Per-image GT diameter (upper bound)
brain (240)0.0050.9250.967 (refine)0.975
intestine (12)0.5440.7730.812 (sizemodel)0.812
colon (10)0.4050.8150.814 (sizemodel) / 0.800 (refine)0.800
pdac (20)0.4190.5640.591 (sizemodel)0.605

Table 1 · E1 segmentation AP50. Zero-shot cyto3 uses its own size model; the "upper bound" gives each image its ground-truth median diameter, which is not available in practice and only separates "scale not estimated" from "model does not recognise".

Three conclusions. First, zero-shot cyto3 recognises organoids (colon recall 0.985) but precision is only 0.4 to 0.6, over-segmentation is severe and AP75 is 0.2 to 0.4; the main failures are scale estimation and boundary quality, and fine-tuning fixes both. Second, the diameter strategies pay off: two-pass inference takes brain from 0.925 to 0.967, almost the ground-truth-diameter bound, and per-image size estimation takes intestine from 0.773 to 0.812. Third, pdac remains weak: test images hold more than 500 small instances each, recall is about 0.5, AP90 is near zero, and even the ground-truth diameter only reaches 0.605, so the problem is the training distribution (68 instances per training image on average, test images from a different instrument) rather than scale.

Cross-organ generalisation. We trained one four-organ joint model and four leave-one-organ-out models. Given the right scale, the joint model matches the specialised ones (with GT diameter: intestine 0.810, pdac 0.606, brain 0.971, colon 0.789; with the usable sizemodel strategy: intestine 0.797, pdac 0.610, colon 0.789, brain refine 0.896), but the training diameter it stores, 183 pixels, is wrong for every single organ, so the model strategy almost completely fails (0.04 to 0.42). Leave-one-out models reach only 0.15 to 0.47 on an organ they have never seen even with the right scale (colon best at 0.465 because it resembles intestine; refine 0.580). Cross-organ generalisation is therefore limited, and organ-specific weights are a necessity rather than a design preference; the joint model serves only as a fallback for unknown organs, where it beats zero-shot cyto3.

Cellpose-SAM comparison. Cellpose-SAM (cellpose 4, ViT-L backbone, advertised as needing no diameter) reaches zero-shot AP50 of about 0.60 on intestine, 0.43 to 0.48 on pdac, about 0.03 on brain and about 0.37 on colon, the same level as zero-shot cyto3, and fails on brain in the same way. After 100 epochs of per-organ fine-tuning it reaches 0.557 on pdac (0.591 with GT diameter) and 0.780 on intestine (0.795), matching but not exceeding fine-tuned cyto3, with weights of 1.2 GB (26 MB for fine-tuned cyto3) and twice the inference time. We therefore keep fine-tuned cyto3 as the main model; the comparison results are preserved in full under results/.

Table 2 · E2 detection. Count MAPE is the mean over images of |predicted − true| / true; total bias is predicted total / true total. Intestine 423 images, brain 280, lung 602.

The joint model matches or slightly beats the single-organ models, so the system keeps one detector. Threshold calibration lowers the counting error on intestine and lung by twenty to thirty percent and corrects the systematic over-count of 10 to 12% at the default threshold to a total bias near 1; brain has one organoid per image and near-zero error at any threshold. The remaining error comes mainly from adjoining clusters and half-organoids at the image edge; a median relative error of 0.11 to 0.13 means most images are off by one or two.

7.3 E3 agreement with expert annotation

The original brain organoid dataset (Schröter et al. 2024) provides, besides masks, a manual area in pixels² per image; we verified that it equals the area of the OrgLine ground-truth mask image by image, so it can serve as an expert reference. 7.4 E4 what quality control contributes

The value of the QC module is that it marks errors rather than removing them. Does it mark the right ones? We tested this on the three organ test sets that have ground-truth masks: for every predicted instance we computed its maximum IoU with any ground-truth instance, called it a wrong instance when IoU was below 0.5 (spurious, fragmented or badly displaced), and looked at how the "low confidence" flag (flip/rotate agreement below 0.5) relates to wrong instances.

OrganPredicted instancesFlagged low-confidenceWrong instances (IoU<0.5)Mean IoU, flaggedMean IoU, restWrong share, flaggedWrong share, restFlag precision / recallSpearman ρ
intestine92310870.400.7860%9%0.60 / 0.070.26
colon70917560.480.8641%7%0.41 / 0.120.35
pdac58571488760.370.6949%14%0.49 / 0.080.29

Table 7-3 · E4 QC flag vs actual segmentation quality (scripts/e4_qc_eval.py, results/e4_qc_eval.json). Precision is the share of flagged instances that are wrong; recall is the share of wrong instances that were flagged; ρ is the rank correlation between agreement and IoU.

On all three organs the instances flagged as low-confidence are indeed much worse: the share of wrong instances among them is 3.5 to 6.8 times that of the remaining instances, and their mean IoU is far lower, so flip/rotate agreement is a genuine reliability signal. Recall, however, is low (0.07 to 0.12): most wrong instances are segmented wrongly in a stable way under flips and rotations, and the many small pdac organoids that are missed altogether never appear as instances at all, so the flag cannot catch what is missing, only what is unstable. The report therefore presents QC as a hint rather than a filter: it directs the user's review effort to the most suspicious instances instead of deciding for the user what to delete.

On the intestinal example image, 120 instances have a mean flip/rotate agreement of 0.98 and only one is flagged, the truncated cluster in the image corner; in the E5 QC task, 3 of 205 instances across 4 intestinal images were flagged.

7.5 E5 end-to-end agent benchmark

We designed 12 natural-language tasks covering single-image analysis, batch analysis with report, analysis with physical pixel size, counting only, group comparison, growth curve, quality control, a follow-up about metric definitions, a follow-up about reproducibility, an unspecified organ, an empty folder and a mixed-organ batch. Each task uses a few of the 36 test images drawn from OrgLine, and success is judged automatically by a script: numbers in the answer must lie within 5 to 10% of the reference values computed by the command-line path, the agreed output files must exist, and key wording must be present (an explanation of circularity must mention the perimeter, an empty folder must be reported as containing no images); for the unspecified-organ task either asking the user or using the generalist model with a caveat is accepted. The runner drives the Agent SDK directly without a terminal, one fresh conversation per task (the two follow-ups run inside their parent task's conversation), with the confirmation mode set to fully automatic.

Table 4 · E5 results, Claude backend (claude-opus-5). Success rate 12/12, 10.5 tool calls per task on average (of which 1.5 are Orgalyst tools; the rest are the task list, file reads and directory checks), 113 s per task, 5.63 US dollars in total.

All 12 tasks passed (this run was completed before the skill of section 5 was added; after adding it we re-ran the batch-analysis, metric-explanation and QC tasks, which all passed again with the mean time falling from 94 s to 72 s, recorded in results/e5_agent_tasks_skilltest.json; a full 12-task re-run is left for the next version). The distribution of tool calls is worth noting: most tasks need one to three calls and the assistant answers straight from the tool's summary, whereas group comparison and growth curve took 31 and 46 calls and 5 to 8 minutes because the assistant read the comparison and growth tables item by item after receiving the statistics and recomputed the medians in Python. This over-checking raises trust but costs time and money; in production it can be constrained through the system prompt. In the unspecified-organ task the assistant did not ask back but ran the generalist model and noted the lower accuracy in its answer, which is consistent with our convention.

8 Reliability analysis and limitations

Failure cases. The two typical segmentation failures both occur at the extreme scales of brain organoids: day-2 organoids only about 80 pixels wide are drowned by the texture of the medium in the first pass, and the second pass of refine then amplifies the error by treating a background patch as the object; day-30 organoids wider than 600 pixels are occasionally cut in two. The pdac failure is systematic: the instance density of the test images is seven times that of the training images and the instrument differs, so the model misses half of the small instances; this needs more in-domain training data or multi-scale inference for small instances, which we did not solve within the competition period. Detection counting merges two adjoining organoids into one and, conversely, counts bubbles and debris.

Cross-organ generalisation boundary. The leave-one-out experiment of section 7.1 gives a clear boundary: on an unseen organ AP50 is only 0.15 to 0.47. The system therefore offers unregistered organs only the generalist model with an explicit low-accuracy notice and promises no accuracy. A new organ should be fine-tuned with a few dozen annotated images (colon went from 0.405 to 0.815 with only 15 training images).

LLM-related risks. The assistant may choose the wrong organ, invent a pixel size, or phrase an uncertain result too confidently. Our mitigation is structural: every number comes from a tool, tool outputs carry their units and exclusion notes, the system prompt forbids estimating an unknown pixel size, and the permission gatekeeper limits file access; the E5 benchmark is the regression test for these constraints. But 12 tasks cannot cover the ways real users phrase requests, we evaluated only the Claude backend, and the gap to open-model backends is not quantified. The assistant also depends on a paid API, so reviewers reproducing the agent path need their own key; the command-line path has no such dependency and reproduces every number in this report.

Data limitations. Only the brain dataset has a pixel calibration, so morphometry for the other organs is in pixels; the OrgLine test sets for intestine (12 images) and colon (10 images) are small and their AP50 confidence intervals are wide; all data come from published public datasets, none from organ-on-a-chip time series, and the growth-curve experiment was validated only on static brain organoid cultures. The correspondence between QC flags and real errors was evaluated only preliminarily on three organ test sets (section 7.4), with limited sample size.

9 Impact and future work

For bench scientists, Orgalyst shortens the path from image to report from half a day to a few minutes, and the report can go into the lab record and still be verified three months later. For method developers, the toolkit provides a framework in which weights and a diameter strategy are registered per organ; adding an organ takes one weight file and one line of configuration. Three things are most valuable next. First, organ-on-a-chip time series: organoids on a chip stay in place, so detection boxes can be linked over time for per-individual tracking instead of relying on metadata in file names as now. Second, dose response: fit four-parameter logistic curves to morphological metrics and check them against known mechanisms of action, the E6 in our design document that we did not reach. Third, integration with laboratory automation: attach the assistant as an MCP client to the scheduling interface of an imaging system so that "analyse automatically after imaging, alert on anomalies" closes the loop. The small-instance problem on pdac deserves its own effort, probably sliding-window multi-scale inference and detection-guided segmentation.

10 Reproduction guide

The repository README gives the full commands; here is the order with expected wall time on an RTX 5090 D. Environment: pip install -r requirements.txt (install torch for your CUDA version; about 10 minutes). Weights: bash scripts/download_weights.sh (about 200 MB; add --mirror in mainland China). Quick check without the dataset: python -m orgalyst analyze --organ intestine --images any_folder_of_brightfield_images --out runs, seconds to tens of seconds. Reproducing all tables: download_orgline.sh and extract_orgline.sh (about 25 GB, depends on bandwidth); prepare_data.py (15 min); run_e1_zeroshot.sh (20 min); run_e1_finetune.sh (2.5 h); run_e1_crossorgan2.sh (3 h); run_e2_det.sh (4.5 h) and calibrate_det_conf.py (15 min); e3_consistency.py (10 min); run_cpsam_ft.sh (needs the separate environment from setup_cellpose4.sh, 2.5 h); e5_prepare.sh and run_agent_tasks.py (needs agent/ and an API key, 25 min, about 6 US dollars). Every script writes to results/; the repository already contains all result files we produced, and every table in this report corresponds to one of them. The Dockerfile covers the command-line path.
